ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The tibial nerve is the larger branch of the sciatic nerve, running down the posterior thigh into the popliteal fossa and then the leg. It supplies motor innervation to the posterior compartment muscles and sensory innervation to the sole of the foot.

b: Largest branch of the sciatic nerve
Forms the medial plantar nerve and lateral plantar nerve in the foot
sections.p: The tibial nerve carries fibers from L4‑S3 and continues the sciatic nerve after it splits at the popliteal fossa. It is essential for plantar flexion, toe flexion and sensation of the sole.

In the popliteal fossa the tibial nerve lies superficial to the popliteal vein and deep to the fascia. It descends posterior to the tibia, passing behind the medial malleolus before entering the foot.
In the popliteal fossa the tibial nerve is superficial to the vein and deep to the fascia; it is accompanied by the posterior tibial artery. Distally it lies medial to the flexor retinaculum.
The tibial nerve receives blood from branches of the popliteal artery proximally and the posterior tibial artery distally.

Motor: gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus, posterior tibialis, intrinsic foot muscles. Sensory: skin of posterior leg, heel, and sole.
Enables plantar flexion, inversion of the foot, and flexion of the toes; provides cutaneous sensation to the posterior leg and plantar surface, crucial for gait stability.

b: Tibial nerve palsy → loss of plantar flexion
Sensory loss on sole may be confused with diabetic neuropathy
sections.p: Compression or trauma to the tibial nerve causes pain, numbness, and weakness in the posterior leg and foot, mimicking peripheral neuropathies. Common causes include popliteal cysts, fractures, and prolonged squatting.

t.b: Confirms site and severity of lesion; slowed conduction indicates demyelination, absent response suggests axonal loss
Detects cysts, tumors, or hematoma compressing the nerve; if unavailable, use bedside ultrasound

b: Weak heel raise suggests tibial nerve injury
Loss of sensation on the plantar surface indicates sensory branch involvement
sections.p: Test plantar flexion strength (heel raise), toe flexion, and sensation on the sole. Compare with the opposite side to detect subtle deficits.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of foot movement after trauma (possible compartment syndrome)
Progressive numbness and weakness with swelling (risk of irreversible nerve damage)
Severe pain unrelieved by analgesia, indicating possible vascular compromise
